So your task is to see if you can extract and disassemble the binary from the disk image, retrieve the display assets, and write a design spec for implementing a fairly faithful recreation inside this repo.

What do you think?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/7.0.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

content.text:
Rod, I like it. Technically it looks very doable, but there's one snag to sort out before I start. If you'd rather skip my questions and have me crack on with extraction and the spec, say so.

**What I checked:**

- The image is a plain 800K HFS floppy: the volume header sits near the start and the name begins "Aft…". Python tools can read HFS, so getting the files out, including the resource forks where the code and graphics live, should be routine.
- I expect the toasters module to be 68000 code plus small bitmap sprites: a few wing-flap frames and the toast. I haven't opened it yet, so that's a guess. Disassembling it would show how it moves things: speeds, spawn rules, the diagonal drift.

**The snag is licensing.** The repo is public and MIT-licensed. AGENTS.md says every copied file needs a licence row, and `check_notices.py` must pass. Berkeley Systems' art and code come with no licence that allows redistribution, and the toasters are among the most fiercely defended screensaver art there is. Berkeley Systems sued Delrina over Opus 'n Bill shooting them down. Committing the extracted sprites, or shipping them in public firmware, would break your own rule, so I'd need your explicit say-so for any exception.

**Ways around it:**

1. **Bring your own disk.** This is the ScummVM approach. Our code reproduces the behaviour, worked out from the disassembly. A build-time tool pulls the sprites from your git-ignored copy of the image, so the repo never holds Berkeley's bytes. Anyone without the image gets a fallback or no toasters.
2. **xscreensaver's `flyingtoasters`.** It's already in `vendor/` under jwz's licence, so it fits our porting pipeline. But it's an XL-sized OpenGL hack with textured 3D toasters, a different look, and probably slow on TinyGL.
3. **Our own pixel art** drawn in the style, with the motion copied from the disassembly.

My instinct is option 1, with option 3's art as the fallback. That keeps the repo clean and still gives you the real toasters on your badge.

Is this just for the board on your lanyard, or do you picture it shipping in the public repo for anyone who builds the firmware?

Option 1 is what I was thinking, and why the disk image is in the (uncommitted) vendor directory.  (BTW, do this work on a worktree, since another agent is currently working in the main checkout here)

# /// script
# dependencies = ["machfs"]
# ///
import sys, struct, os
from machfs import Volume
v = Volume(); v.read(open(sys.argv[1], "rb").read())
out = sys.argv[2]
def get(path):
    x = v
    for p in path.split("/"): x = x[p]
    return x
def parse(r):
    doff, moff, dlen, mlen = struct.unpack(">IIII", r[:16])
    m = r[moff:moff+mlen]
    tloff, nloff = struct.unpack(">HH", m[24:28])
    tl = m[tloff:]
    n = struct.unpack(">H", tl[:2])[0] + 1
    res = []
    for i in range(n):
        t, cnt, roff = struct.unpack(">4sHH", tl[2+i*8:10+i*8])
        for j in range(cnt+1):
            e = tl[roff + j*12: roff + j*12 + 12]
            rid, nameoff, attr_off = struct.unpack(">hhI", e[:8])
            o = attr_off & 0xFFFFFF
            ln = struct.unpack(">I", r[doff+o:doff+o+4])[0]
            body = r[doff+o+4:doff+o+4+ln]
            name = ""
            if nameoff != -1:
                nl = m[nloff+nameoff]; name = m[nloff+nameoff+1:nloff+nameoff+1+nl].decode("mac_roman")
            res.append((t.decode("mac_roman"), rid, name, body))
    return res
for path in sys.argv[3:]:
    f = get(path)
    d = os.path.join(out, path.split("/")[-1].replace(" ", "_").replace("!", ""))
    os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)
    open(os.path.join(d, "data.bin"), "wb").write(f.data)
    for t, rid, name, body in parse(f.rsrc):
        safe = t.replace(" ", "_").replace("#", "H").replace("/", "_")
        open(os.path.join(d, f"{safe}_{rid}.bin"), "wb").write(body)
        print(f"{path.split('/')[-1]:20} {t!r} {rid:6} {len(body):6} {name!r}")
EOF

# dependencies = ["machfs"]
# ///
import os
import struct
import sys

from machfs import Volume

v = Volume()
v.read(open(sys.argv[1], "rb").read())
out = sys.argv[2]


def get(path):
    x = v
    for p in path.split("/"):
        x = x[p]
    return x


def parse(r):
    doff, moff, dlen, mlen = struct.unpack(">IIII", r[:16])
    m = r[moff : moff + mlen]
    tloff, nloff = struct.unpack(">HH", m[24:28])
    tl = m[tloff:]
    n = struct.unpack(">H", tl[:2])[0] + 1
    res = []
    for i in range(n):
        t, cnt, roff = struct.unpack(">4sHH", tl[2 + i * 8 : 10 + i * 8])
        for j in range(cnt + 1):
            e = tl[roff + j * 12 : roff + j * 12 + 12]
            rid, nameoff, attr_off = struct.unpack(">hhI", e[:8])
            o = attr_off & 0xFFFFFF
            ln = struct.unpack(">I", r[doff + o : doff + o + 4])[0]
            body = r[doff + o + 4 : doff + o + 4 + ln]
            name = ""
            if nameoff != -1:
                nl = m[nloff + nameoff]
                name = m[nloff + nameoff + 1 : nloff + nameoff + 1 + nl].decode("mac_roman")
            res.append((t.decode("mac_roman"), rid, name, body))
    return res


for path in sys.argv[3:]:
    f = get(path)
    leaf = path.split("/")[-1]
    d = os.path.join(out, leaf.replace(" ", "_").replace("!", ""))
    os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)
    if f.data:
        open(os.path.join(d, "data.bin"), "wb").write(f.data)
    if not f.rsrc:
        continue
    for t, rid, name, body in parse(f.rsrc):
        safe = t.replace(" ", "_").replace("#", "H").replace("/", "_")
        open(os.path.join(d, f"{safe}_{rid}.bin"), "wb").write(body)
        print(f"{leaf:22} {t!r} {rid:6} {len(body):6} {name!r}")

# /// script
# dependencies = ["pillow"]
# ///
"""Minimal PICT v1/v2 decoder: enough for PackBitsRect / BitsRect sprites."""

import struct
import sys

from PIL import Image


def unpackbits(src, n):
    out = bytearray()
    i = 0
    while len(out) < n:
        c = src[i]
        i += 1
        if c < 128:
            out += src[i : i + c + 1]
            i += c + 1
        elif c > 128:
            out += bytes([src[i]]) * (257 - c)
            i += 1
    return bytes(out[:n]), i


def read_rect(b, p):
    return struct.unpack(">hhhh", b[p : p + 8])


def decode(b):
    p = 2 + 8
    v2 = b[p : p + 2] == b"\x00\x11"
    p += 2 if v2 else 0
    images = []
    log = []

    def opcode():
        nonlocal p
        if v2:
            p += p & 1
            op = struct.unpack(">H", b[p : p + 2])[0]
            p += 2
        else:
            op = b[p]
            p += 1
        return op

    while p < len(b):
        start = p
        op = opcode()
        log.append(f"{start:04x}:{op:04x}")
        if op in (0x11,) and not v2:
            p += 1
        elif op == 0x02FF:
            p += 2
        elif op == 0x0C00:
            p += 24
        elif op == 0x001E:
            pass
        elif op == 0x0001:
            ln = struct.unpack(">H", b[p : p + 2])[0]
            p += ln
        elif op == 0x00A0:
            p += 2
        elif op == 0x00A1:
            p += 2
            ln = struct.unpack(">H", b[p : p + 2])[0]
            p += 2 + ln
        elif op == 0x001A or op == 0x001B or op == 0x001F:
            p += 6
        elif op in (0x0090, 0x0098, 0x009A):
            if op == 0x009A:
                p += 4
            rb = struct.unpack(">H", b[p : p + 2])[0]
            pixmap = bool(rb & 0x8000) or op == 0x009A
            rowbytes = rb & 0x3FFF
            p += 2
            top, left, bottom, right = read_rect(b, p)
            p += 8
            w, h = right - left, bottom - top
            clut = None
            depth = 1
            if pixmap:
                (_ver, pack_type, _psz, _hr, _vr, _ptype, depth, _cc, _cs, _pt, _tab, _res) = struct.unpack(
                    ">hhIiihhhhIII", b[p : p + 36]
                )
                p += 36
                if op != 0x009A:
                    _seed, _flags, n = struct.unpack(">IHH", b[p : p + 8])
                    p += 8
                    clut = {}
                    for i in range(n + 1):
                        idx, r, g, bl = struct.unpack(">HHHH", b[p : p + 8])
                        clut[i if _flags & 0x8000 else idx] = (r >> 8, g >> 8, bl >> 8)
                        p += 8
            src = read_rect(b, p)
            dst = read_rect(b, p + 8)
            mode = struct.unpack(">h", b[p + 16 : p + 18])[0]
            p += 18
            rows = []
            for _ in range(h):
                if rowbytes < 8:
                    rows.append(b[p : p + rowbytes])
                    p += rowbytes
                else:
                    if rowbytes > 250:
                        bc = struct.unpack(">H", b[p : p + 2])[0]
                        p += 2
                    else:
                        bc = b[p]
                        p += 1
                    row, _ = unpackbits(b[p : p + bc], rowbytes)
                    rows.append(row)
                    p += bc
            img = Image.new("RGBA", (w, h))
            px = img.load()
            for y, row in enumerate(rows):
                for x in range(w):
                    if depth == 1:
                        bit = (row[x >> 3] >> (7 - (x & 7))) & 1
                        px[x, y] = (0, 0, 0, 255) if bit else (255, 255, 255, 255)
                    else:
                        per = 8 // depth
                        v = (row[x // per] >> ((per - 1 - x % per) * depth)) & ((1 << depth) - 1)
                        r, g, bl = clut.get(v, (255, 0, 255))
                        px[x, y] = (r, g, bl, 255)
            images.append(dict(op=op, depth=depth, bounds=(top, left, bottom, right), src=src, dst=dst, mode=mode, img=img, ncol=len(clut) if clut else 0))
        elif op == 0x00FF:
            break
        else:
            log.append(f"UNKNOWN op {op:04x} at {start:04x}")
            break
    return images, log


if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = sys.argv[1]
    for path in sys.argv[2:]:
        data = open(path, "rb").read()
        images, log = decode(data)
        name = path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1].removesuffix(".bin")
        print(name, " ".join(log))
        for i, im in enumerate(images):
            print(f"  img{i} op={im['op']:04x} depth={im['depth']} bounds={im['bounds']} dst={im['dst']} mode={im['mode']} colours={im['ncol']}")
            im["img"].resize((im["img"].width * 4, im["img"].height * 4), Image.NEAREST).save(f"{out}/{name}_{i}.png")

"""Throwaway: one still frame of colour toasters on the 466 px round panel."""

import random
import sys

from PIL import Image, ImageDraw

png_dir, out_dir = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]

        tries += 1
        x, y = random.randrange(0, 466 - size), random.randrange(0, 466 - size)

        placed.append((x, y))
    for i, (x, y) in enumerate(placed):
        sprite = frames[4] if i % 4 == 3 else frames[i % 4]
        canvas.paste(sprite.resize((size, size), Image.NEAREST), (x, y))
    mask = Image.new("L", (466, 466), 0)

Rod, extraction and disassembly both worked, and I've opened three pictures in Preview for you: the decoded sprite sheet and two mockups of the round screen.

**What's on the disk:**

- The image is an 800K HFS floppy with a 12-byte tag on every sector; strip those and it reads cleanly.
- The Flying Toasters module has four wing-flap frames and the toast, each 64×64, in both 1-bit and 16-colour versions. It also has three flap sounds and 12 KB of 68000 code.
- Every routine still carries its debugger name, which made the disassembly far easier to follow.
- The disk also has Berkeley's module SDK, which defines the calling convention. Its three main calls match our runner's init, draw and free.

**How the original behaves** (I checked the starred items in the code myself; the rest comes from the subagent's reading and agrees with what I saw):

- ★ It steps at most 30 times a second.
- ★ The number of flyers is the slider value divided by 5: 10 at the default, up to 20.
- ★ A quarter are toast, at speed 1. The rest are toasters at speed 1, 2 or 3, about a quarter each.
- ★ Each step moves a flyer speed × (2 px left, 1 px down).
- ★ The wings flap 0,1,2,3,2,1, one frame per step, and every toaster starts on frame 0.
- ★ Flyers first scatter across the screen. After that they enter from just above the top or just past the right edge, half and half, with up to 4 tries to avoid overlapping another flyer.
- There's no transparency mask. Each sprite is drawn as an opaque 70×70 block with a black border on the top and right that wipes its own trail, and flyers simply avoid overlapping.
- The "Toast:" slider sets doneness, not how much toast there is. Medium and Dark subtract a fixed grey from the toast's colours.

**My plan, which is my call so far:** our own hack, MIT-licensed. A build step reads the sprites from your git-ignored image, the same way `pacman_sprites.py` handles Pac-Man's art. If the image is missing, the hack is simply left out of the build, and host tests use stand-in sprites.

What's wrong or missing there? Also, looking at the two mockups: should the toasters keep their original 64-pixel size (1×, which is about the scale they had on a compact Mac's screen), or be doubled to chunky 128-pixel ones (2×) to suit the small round screen?

For your question, I think the 1x version looks best.

Other than that, I think you're good to start continue.

74	
75	| Index | Control | Use |
76	| --- | --- | --- |
77	| 0 | sVal 1000 "Flying objects:" (default 54) | `n = max(1, v / 5)` (0x3e2-0x3fe). Default 54 gives 10. A 0-100 slider gives 1-20, matching sUnt 1000's labels "1".."20". **certain** for the formula, **likely** for the 0-100 range |

79	| 2 | xVal 1002 "Color" (default 1) | colour art if `v == 1` and `colorQDAvail` (0x3c2-0x3da). **certain** |
80	| 3 | none | never read. µVal 1001/1002 (= 3) are not referenced by the code; their meaning is unresolved |
81	
82	DoDrawFrame returns result 1 (restart) when cv0 changes, cv2 changes, or cv1
83	changes while colour is on (0xcf2-0xd2c). **certain**

85	## 1. Frame pacing
86	
87	```c
88	// DoDrawFrame 0xcd0
89	if (sndExt && TickCount() >= nextSound) { ... }          // see section 7
90	if (TickCount() >= nextStep) {                           // 0xd90
91	    nextStep = TickCount() + 2;
92	    AdvanceFlyers(blankRgn->rgnBBox);
93	}
94	```
95	
96	- One simulation step per 2 ticks: at most **30 steps/s**. No catch-up: a
97	  slow step just delays the next. **certain**
98	- Every step moves and draws every flyer. There's no per-frame work limit.
99	  **certain**
100	
101	## 2. Flyer creation
102	
103	```c
104	// CreateFlyers 0xf10 (DoInitialize, with running = 0)
105	for (i = 0; i < n; i++) flyers[i] = CreateFlyer(i, rect = spriteRect, bounds);
106	
107	// CreateFlyer 0xdf8: bounds = blank region's bounding box
108	tries = 4;
109	do {
110	    if (running) RandomRectEdge(bounds, &rect);      // 0x1458
111	    else         RandomRectInside(bounds, &rect);    // 0x1538
112	} while (Collision(i, &rect) && --tries);
113	if (tries == 0) return NULL;                         // slot stays empty
114	r = abs(Random() % 100);                             // 0..99
115	if (r >= 75) { t = new Toast;   InitToast(t, rect); }        // 25 %
116	else         { t = new Toaster; InitToaster(t, rect, r); }   // 75 %
117	return t;
118	```
119	
120	- Toast probability is a fixed 25%. The "Toast:" slider does not affect it.
121	  **certain**
122	- Up to 4 placement attempts. If all collide, the slot is NULL and is retried
123	  at the start of every later step (AdvanceFlyers pass 1). **certain**
124	- `RandomRectInside` 0x1538 (initial population only): uniform placement
125	  fully inside the bounds:
126	  `top = bounds.top + abs(Random() % (H - 70))`, then
127	  `left = bounds.left + abs(Random() % (W - 70))` (the y draw comes first).
128	  **certain**
129	- `RandomRectEdge` 0x1458 (every later spawn): `if (Random() % 2 != 0)`,
130	  i.e. odd, about 50%:
131	  - **top edge**: `rect.bottom = bounds.top`,
132	    `rect.left = bounds.left + abs(Random() % W)`;
133	  - **else right edge**: `rect.left = bounds.right`,
134	    `rect.top = bounds.top + abs(Random() % H)`.
135	
136	  The rect is the 70x70 sprite rect. So a top spawn has x anywhere across
137	  the full width, including near the left edge where it leaves almost at
138	  once. **certain**
139	- Colour versus mono doesn't change spawning. **certain**
140	- `abs(Random() % k)`: Toolbox Random is -32767..32767 and `divs` keeps the
141	  dividend's sign, so 0 is roughly twice as likely as any other value.
142	  That's a negligible bias. **certain**
143	
144	## 3. Motion
145	
146	```c
147	// InitFlying 0x12aa: r = rect; speed = 1
148	// InitToaster 0x130e: speed = r >= 50 ? 3 : r >= 25 ? 2 : 1;
149	//                     frame = 0; flapDown = 0
150	// InitToast 0x13f4:  speed = 1
151	
152	// AdvanceFlyers 0x1066 (bounds = blank bbox)
153	for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {                        // pass 1
154	    if (!flyers[i]) flyers[i] = CreateFlyer(i, spriteRect, bounds);
155	    if (flyers[i]) OffsetRect(&flyers[i]->r, -2, +1);   // base step, no check
156	}
157	for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {                        // pass 2
158	    f = flyers[i]; if (!f) continue;
159	    if (!SectRect(f->r, bounds)) { Dispose(f); flyers[i] = NULL; continue; }
160	    s = f->speed - 1;
161	    if (s > 0) {
162	        cand = f->r; OffsetRect(&cand, -2*s, +s);
163	        if ((p = Collision(i, &cand)) != NULL) {
164	            cand = f->r;                          // back to base-step position
165	            OffsetRect(&cand, p->h * 1, p->v * -2);
166	            if (!Collision(i, &cand)) f->r = cand;   // else keep base step
167	        } else f->r = cand;
168	    }
169	    f->Draw();                                    // drawn right after its move
170	}
171	```
172	
173	- Per step, `(dx, dy) = speed * (-2, +1)`: left 2 px and down 1 px per speed
174	  unit. The heading is down-left at a 2:1 slope (about 26.6 degrees below
175	  horizontal). **certain**
176	- Speeds: toast is always 1. Toasters get 1, 2 or 3 with equal odds
177	  (r 0-24, 25-49, 50-74). Overall: 25% toast at speed 1, and 25% each
178	  toaster at speed 1, 2 and 3. At 30 steps/s, speed 1 is 60 px/s left and
179	  30 px/s down; speed 3 is 180 and 90. The speed is fixed for the flyer's
180	  life. No control affects speed. **certain**
181	- Leaving the screen: once the 70x70 rect no longer intersects the bounds,
182	  the flyer is disposed. Its slot respawns at the next step at the top or
183	  right edge (pass 1), as a fresh random toast or toaster. **certain**
184	- Only speed-2 and speed-3 toasters ever test for collisions while moving.
185	  Speed-1 flyers (and all toast) move blindly. **certain**
186	- `Collision(i, cand)` 0xf6e: the first other non-NULL flyer `o` whose rect
187	  intersects `cand` (`SectRect` result non-empty) gives:
188	  - `dl = o.left - cand.left`, `dt = o.top - cand.top`;
189	  - if `|dt| < |dl|`: `p = (v -1, h 0)`. With the nudge applied as
190	    `(h*1, v*-2)`, the flyer drops **2 px further down** this step (net
191	    `(-2, +3)`);
192	  - else: `p.h = (cand.top < o.top) ? -1 : +1`, `p.v = 0`. If it's above
193	    the other flyer it moves 1 px further left (net `(-3, +1)`), otherwise
194	    1 px less (net `(-1, +1)`).
195	  - Returns NULL when there's no overlap. **certain**
196	- A nudge never exceeds 6 px left or 6 px down, so the black margin still
197	  erases the trail (section 6). **certain**
198	
199	## 4. Animation (Toaster.Draw 0x1360)
200	
201	```c
202	CopyBits(frames[frame], screen, spriteRect, r, srcCopy, NULL);
203	if (flapDown) { if (frame == 0) { frame = 1; flapDown = 0; } else frame--; }
204	else          { if (frame == 3) { frame = 2; flapDown = 1; } else frame++; }
205	```
206	
207	- Frame sequence (ping-pong, period 6): **0 1 2 3 2 1 0 1 2 3 2 1 ...**,
208	  with PICTs 128+frame (mono) or 228+frame (colour). **certain**
209	- The frame advances once per Draw. Draw runs once per step (and once in
210	  DoBlank), so the frame advances every step: 30 frames/s and 5 wing beats
211	  per second. It's the same for every toaster speed. **certain**
212	- No per-toaster phase offset: every toaster starts at frame 0, going up.
213	  The random 0-99 from CreateFlyer only chooses the speed. The phases differ
214	  only because toasters spawn on different steps. **certain**
215	
216	## 5. Doneness (DoInitialize 0x9d4-0xa3c, colour mode only)
217	
218	After drawing PICT 232 into the toast's offscreen buffer (filled black
219	first):
220	
221	```c
222	if (color) {
223	    OpColor(&(RGBColor){0, 0, 0});           // pin = black
224	    if (cv1 >= 33) {
225	        rgb = (cv1 < 67) ? (RGBColor){0x4fff, 0x4fff, 0x4fff}   // Medium
226	                         : (RGBColor){0x7fff, 0x6fff, 0x6fff};  // Dark
227	        RGBForeColor(&rgb); PenMode(35 /* subPin */);
228	        PaintRect(&toastRect /* incl. 6 px margin */);
229	    }
230	}
231	```
232	
233	- The rule per channel, in 16-bit units: `c' = max(c - k, 0)`. In 8-bit
234	  terms: Medium subtracts about 80 from R, G and B; Dark subtracts about 128
235	  from R and about 112 from G and B. Light (cv1 < 33) is unchanged. The
236	  black background stays black. **certain** for the operation. The
237	  thresholds 33 and 67 assume a 0-100 slider (**likely**).
238	- QuickDraw does the arithmetic on the RGB of each colour-table entry and
239	  maps the result back to the nearest index at the buffer's depth (the
240	  deepest monitor's). On an 8-bit screen the result is quantised to the
241	  palette. **likely**
242	- Mono mode: no doneness at all. The 1-bit toast (PICT 132) is drawn as is.
243	  **certain**
244	
245	## 6. Drawing
246	
247	- Each sprite has an offscreen buffer the size of `spriteRect` = 70x70: the
248	  64x64 PICT at buffer (0..63, 6..69), with a **6-px black strip along the
249	  top and a 6-px strip down the right** (buffer filled with QD black, then
250	  DrawPicture). **certain**
251	- Draw = plain `CopyBits(..., srcCopy, maskRgn = NULL)` of the whole 70x70
252	  rect to the screen port (base `Pix.CopyTo` 0x1934; the receiver is the
253	  screen object, whose class doesn't override it). **There is no mask:**
254	  black pixels in the art are opaque. `CalcMonoMask` and `CalcColorMask`
255	  (names really `CALCMONO` / `CALCCOLO`) only compute buffer byte sizes for
256	  the memory estimate (rowBytes x height, + 0x5ea for mono). **certain**
257	- No dirty-rect erase and no full-screen buffer. Motion is at most 6 px left
258	  and 6 px down per step, so the black top and right strips of the new copy
259	  cover everything the old copy left behind. **certain**
260	- Overlap is handled by keeping the 70x70 rects apart (spawn retries plus
261	  fast-toaster nudges), not by masking. When flyers do overlap (a speed-1
262	  flyer drifting into another, a failed nudge), the later index's black box
263	  overwrites the earlier one. **certain** (mechanism); how often it happens
264	  is unmeasured.
265	- Z-order = slot index order. Each flyer is drawn right after its own move
266	  in pass 2, so higher indices are on top. **certain**
267	- Background: DoBlank fills the blank region black (`FillRgn(blankRgn,
268	  qd.black)`), calls FixClipping, then draws every flyer once (which also
269	  advances each toaster to frame 1). **certain**
270	- FixClipping 0x1678 sets the clip to the union of all monitor rects, each
271	  with `top + 1` (one pixel row dropped at the top of every screen).
272	  **certain** (code). The purpose is a **guess**.
273	
274	## 7. Sound
275	
276	- Only if After Dark's sound extension ('ADsd' in `params->extensions`,
277	  found by 0x294e) is present: 0x282e sets 0x2a78. Snd 128-130 are loaded
278	  and each one's length is taken from the extension (0x2904, a vtable call
279	  near "GetSoundLength"). **likely**
280	- DoDrawFrame 0xd30: `if (TickCount() >= nextSound) { play(snd[cur]);
281	  nextSound = TickCount() + len[cur]; cur = Shuffle(cur, 0, 2); }`. Shuffle
282	  0x1648 draws `abs(Random()) % 3` until the result differs from `cur`.
283	  **certain**
284	- So it's a continuous back-to-back soundtrack of Flap 1, Flap 2 and Mix 1
285	  in random order, never the same one twice in a row. It starts with Flap 1
286	  (cur = 0, nextSound = 0). It isn't tied to individual toasters. **certain**
287	  for the logic. That `len` is in ticks is **likely**, since it's added to
288	  TickCount.
289	
290	## 8. Other notes
291	
292	- Everything is in pixels with fixed 64x64 art. The screen size enters only
293	  through `bounds` (the blank region's bounding box) for spawning and
294	  culling, and through the clip. **certain**
295	- Max flyers: 20 with a 0-100 slider (n = v / 5). There's no other cap;
296	  memory is checked up front (0x400 + 16n + 5 x buffer size + snd sizes).
297	  **certain** (formula)
298	- Demo rect: not read by this module. In the preview, the blank region is
299	  just smaller, and the same rules apply. **likely**
300	- Colour buffers are created at the deepest monitor's depth (0x382-0x3c0
301	  scans the monitors for min and max depth; max is passed on). **certain**
302	- Requires After Dark 2.0 (0x29d4 with 0x200) and `systemConfig` bit 14
303	  ("2.0u or newer"). **certain**
304	
305	## Recreation checklist (466 x 466 round)
306	
307	- Step at 30 Hz. Bounds = 466 x 466 square (the culling and spawn logic are
308	  rect-based; spawning off-screen corners of the circle is faithful).
309	- 70x70 rects, 64x64 art at (+0, +6), 6-px black margin top and right, opaque
310	  black.
311	- Slots n = max(1, v/5), default 10. Initial: uniform inside. Respawn: 50% top
312	  edge (any x), 50% right edge (any y), 4 tries per step.
313	- 25% toast (speed 1). Toasters have speed 1, 2 or 3 with equal odds. Step
314	  `speed*(-2,+1)`, with the collision nudge for speed > 1 only.
315	- Flap 0,1,2,3,2,1 once per step, starting at 0.
316	- Doneness in colour: subtract (80,80,80) or (128,112,112), clamped at 0.
317	
318	## Open questions
319	
320	- The slider's value range is assumed to be 0-100 (After Dark's standard).
321	  The thresholds 33 and 67, and n up to 20, depend on it. µVal 1001/1002
322	  (= 3) are unused by the code and may be the slider's tick or unit counts
323	  for the dialog.
324	- Sound length units come from the extension's function and aren't
325	  verified.
326	- Exactly how QuickDraw's subPin quantises the toast at 4- and 8-bit depth
327	  depends on the screen's colour table. A modern recreation should do the
328	  subtraction on the toast art's RGB directly.
329	- The reason for FixClipping's `top + 1` isn't known.
330	- How often flyers overlap visibly in practice wasn't simulated.

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Code Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Text Block]
[EOF]
```

Every block transition = blank line required.

## Quick Patterns

**List:**

```markdown

- item

```

**Heading:**

```markdown

## Head

```

**Code:**

````markdown
text

```

````

**Nested:**

```markdown
- parent
  - child
- parent
```

**Ordered:**

```markdown
text

1. item
1. item

text
```

**Table:**

```markdown
text

| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| Cell | Cell |

text
```

## Common Languages

**Programming:** `python` `javascript` `java` `c` `cpp` `go` `rust` `ruby`
`php` `swift` `kotlin` `typescript`

**Shell:** `bash` `sh` `powershell` `cmd` `zsh`

**Markup:** `html` `css` `xml` `json` `yaml` `toml` `markdown`

**Database:** `sql` `postgresql` `mysql`

**Other:** `text` `diff` `log`

## Validation

```bash
markdownlint filename.md
```

Goal: Zero errors/warnings.

## Additional Resources

See bundled references:

- `references/complete-rules.md` - Full rule catalog
- `references/edge-cases.md` - Platform quirks
- `references/examples.md` - Detailed examples

## Remember

Most common: Missing blank lines around lists/headings/code.

**Two trailing spaces:** Intentional line breaks. Do NOT remove.

1. Add blank lines before/after blocks
2. Use `-` for lists
3. Use `#` for headings
4. Specify code language
5. Increment headings by one
6. Use regular spaces only

# Flying Toasters from After Dark 2.0: design

## Intent

Bring back After Dark's Flying Toasters, the classic 1990 Mac screensaver,
on the StopWatch, as faithfully as the hardware allows: the original art,
moving to the original rules. Rod owns a copy of After Dark 2.0 on an 800K
floppy image. This is a nostalgia piece for his own badge, in the same spirit
as Pyro was for the xscreensaver hacks.

The art and code are Berkeley Systems' copyright and carry no licence to
redistribute. The repo is public and MIT. So the design follows the
ScummVM model: **our code reproduces the behaviour; the art is read at build
time from the user's own disk image, which is never committed.** Anyone
without the image gets a build with no toasters in it.

## Goals

- A new hack, `toasters`, that reproduces Flying Toasters' motion, spawning,
  wing-flap animation, collision nudging and toast doneness, worked out from
  the original 68000 code (see "Behaviour" below).
- The original sprites, extracted at build time from
  `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k`.
- Each time the hack starts it picks, at random:
  - the **1-bit** or the **16-colour** art (even odds);
  - the toast **doneness**: Light, Medium or Dark (even odds).

  This is Rod's request: the original made these user settings.
- Sprites at their original size, 64×64 (1×). Rod chose this over 2× from
  mockups of the round panel.
- Builds without the disk image still succeed, and simply leave the hack out.

## Non-goals

- Sound. The original plays its flap sounds through After Dark's sound
  extension; the board has no speaker, and sound is a non-goal for the whole
  project. The rule is recorded below for completeness only.
- User settings at run time (count, colour, doneness sliders). Count stays at
  the original's default; colour and doneness are random per start.
- Other After Dark modules. The disk holds 30-odd; they may follow later, and
  the extraction tool should not make that harder, but this design covers
  only Flying Toasters.
- Porting xscreensaver's `flyingtoasters` (jwz's OpenGL tribute). It is a
  different look and an XL GL port; it stays unported.

## Anti-goals

These would make it a failure even if it worked:

- **Any Berkeley Systems bytes in git**: no sprites, no PICT data, no
  disassembly listings, no test fixtures cut from the disk. That includes
  test data and docs. Behavioural descriptions and code offsets (as in this
  document) are fine.
- A build that fails for someone without the disk image.
- Publishing a firmware binary that contains the art. (None are published
  today; keep it that way for builds that include the toasters.)
- "Improving" the original's look: no alpha masks, no smoothing, no scaling.
  The black box around each sprite is part of how the original works, and
  stays.

## What is on the disk

Found during the investigation that led to this design (scratch work, not
committed):

- `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k` is 838,400 bytes: 1600 sectors of 524
  bytes, each 512 data bytes followed by a 12-byte tag (a raw floppy dump with
  sector tags, not DiskCopy 4.2). Dropping the tags gives an 819,200-byte HFS
  volume named "After Dark™ Disk".
- `After Dark Files/Flying Toasters` is an `ADgm`/`ADrk` file with an empty
  data fork. Its resource fork holds:

  | Resource | Contents |
  | --- | --- |
  | `PICT` 128-131 | 1-bit toaster frames 0-3, 64×64 |
  | `PICT` 132 | 1-bit toast, 64×64 |
  | `PICT` 228-231 | 16-colour toaster frames 0-3, 64×64 (PICT v2, 4-bit indexed, own colour table) |
  | `PICT` 232 | 16-colour toast, 64×64 |
  | `ADgm` 0 | the module's 68000 code (12,402 bytes, Think C, MacsBug names intact) |
  | `snd` 128-130 | "Flap 1", "Flap 2", "Mix 1" |
  | `sVal`/`xVal`/`sUnt` | control defaults: count slider 54, toast doneness 0 (Light), colour on |
  | `TEXT` 1000, `STR` 128 | credits |

- All ten PICTs are a single PackBitsRect opcode (`0x98`). The 1-bit ones
  are PICT v1 whose bitmap is 72 px wide with 4 px either side outside the
  64×64 `picFrame`; draw them through the frame, as `DrawPicture` would, and
  the extra columns fall away. In the 1-bit art a set bit is black: the
  pictures are white line art on black.
- Credits from the module: Jack Eastman, Bruce Burkhalter and Patrick Beard,
  artwork by Tomoya Ikeda, ©1990-91 Berkeley Systems Inc. The hack's header
  comment should name them.

## Behaviour

Read from the `ADgm` code. Offsets are into that resource. Everything here
is **certain** (read directly from the code) unless marked otherwise.
Coordinates are QuickDraw's: x right, y down. Rect is (top, left, bottom,
right).

### Pacing

- One simulation step per two 60 Hz ticks: at most **30 steps a second**
  (`DoDrawFrame` 0xd90: step when `TickCount() >= next`, then
  `next = TickCount() + 2`). A late step is not caught up.
- Every step moves and draws every flyer.

### Flyers

- Slot count `n = max(1, countSlider / 5)` (0x3e2). The default slider of
  54 gives **10**, which we use.
- Each flyer owns a **70×70 rect**: the 64×64 art plus a 6 px black strip
  along its top and a 6 px strip down its right. In sprite-local terms the
  rect is (top −6, left 0, bottom 64, right 70) and the art sits at
  (0..63, 0..63).
- Creating a flyer (`CreateFlyer` 0xdf8):

  ```c
  tries = 4;
  do {
      rect = running ? random_edge_rect(bounds) : random_inside_rect(bounds);
  } while (collides(i, rect) && --tries);
  if (tries == 0) return NULL;          /* slot stays empty; retried next step */
  r = abs(Random() % 100);              /* 0..99 */
  if (r >= 75) return toast(rect);      /* speed 1 */
  return toaster(rect, speed = r >= 50 ? 3 : r >= 25 ? 2 : 1);
  ```

  So 25% each: toast, slow toaster, medium toaster, fast toaster. Speed is
  fixed for a flyer's life.
- `random_inside_rect` (0x1538), used once, at start: the rect fully
  inside the bounds, `top = abs(Random() % (H − 70))` first, then
  `left = abs(Random() % (W − 70))`.
- `random_edge_rect` (0x1458), every later spawn: with even odds, either
  **just above the top edge** (`rect.bottom = bounds.top`, left anywhere in
  `abs(Random() % W)`) or **just past the right edge**
  (`rect.left = bounds.right`, top anywhere in `abs(Random() % H)`).
- Toolbox `Random()` returns −32767..32767 and `%` keeps the sign, hence the
  `abs`. Use our `random()`; the tiny bias towards 0 need not be copied.

### Motion

Per step (`AdvanceFlyers` 0x1066), in two passes over the slots:

```c
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {                       /* pass 1 */
    if (!flyer[i]) flyer[i] = create_flyer(i);
    if (flyer[i]) offset(&flyer[i]->r, -2, +1); /* base step, unchecked */
}
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {                       /* pass 2 */
    f = flyer[i]; if (!f) continue;
    if (!intersects(f->r, bounds)) { flyer[i] = NULL; continue; }
    s = f->speed - 1;
    if (s > 0) {
        cand = f->r; offset(&cand, -2 * s, +s);
        if ((p = collision(i, cand))) {
            cand = f->r; offset(&cand, p.h, -2 * p.v);
            if (!collision(i, cand)) f->r = cand;   /* else keep base step */
        } else f->r = cand;
    }
    draw(f);                                    /* drawn straight after its move */
}
```

- Net motion is `speed × (−2, +1)` px per step: down and to the left at a
  2:1 slope. Speed 1 is 60 px/s left and 30 px/s down at 30 steps/s.
- Only speed 2 and 3 toasters check for collisions. Toast and speed-1
  toasters move blindly.
- `collision(i, cand)` (0xf6e) looks for the first other flyer `o` whose
  rect intersects `cand`, and returns a nudge `p`:
  - if `|o.top − cand.top| < |o.left − cand.left|` (mostly beside it):
    `p = (v −1, h 0)`, which as applied above drops the flyer 2 px further
    down this step;
  - otherwise `p = (v 0, h cand.top < o.top ? −1 : +1)`: 1 px further left
    if it is above `o`, 1 px less far left if below.
- A flyer is removed once its rect no longer touches the bounds. Its slot
  respawns on the next step's pass 1.
- `bounds` is the whole screen: for us the 466×466 square. Spawning and
  dying in the circle's hidden corners is faithful and harmless.

### Animation

`Toaster.Draw` (0x1360) draws the current frame, then advances:

```c
blit(frames[frame], f->r);
if (flap_down) { if (frame == 0) { frame = 1; flap_down = 0; } else frame--; }
else           { if (frame == 3) { frame = 2; flap_down = 1; } else frame++; }
```

- The sequence is **0 1 2 3 2 1 0 1 …**, one frame per step: 5 wing beats a
  second at every speed.
- Every toaster starts at frame 0 going up. There is no random phase.
  Toasters differ in phase only because they spawn on different steps.

### Drawing

- **There is no mask.** Each flyer is an opaque copy of its 70×70 rect,
  black included. No step moves a flyer more than 6 px left or down, so the
  black strips on the top and right wipe the trail of the previous position.
  There is no erase pass and no back buffer.
- Overlap is avoided by spacing (spawn retries, nudges), not hidden by
  masking. When flyers do overlap, the later slot's black box covers the
  earlier one. That is faithful; keep it.
- Draw order is slot order, higher slots on top.
- At start the screen is filled black and every flyer drawn once (`DoBlank`
  0xc40), which also advances each toaster to frame 1.
- The original clips one pixel row off the top of each monitor
  (`FixClipping` 0x1678); the reason is unknown and we skip it.

### Colour and doneness

- 1-bit mode draws PICTs 128-132 as white on black. 16-colour mode draws
  228-232 through their colour tables.
- Doneness applies **only in colour mode**, once at start, to the toast's
  pixels (0x9d4-0xa3c): QuickDraw's `subPin` mode, `c' = max(c − k, 0)` per
  channel, with:

  | Doneness | k (16-bit RGB) | About, in 8-bit |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Light | none | unchanged |
  | Medium | 0x4fff, 0x4fff, 0x4fff | 80, 80, 80 |
  | Dark | 0x7fff, 0x6fff, 0x6fff | 128, 112, 112 |

  Do the subtraction on the toast's RGB888 before converting to RGB565.
  Black stays black.
- In 1-bit mode doneness has no effect, as in the original. The random pick
  is still made, so the log can show it, but the toast looks the same.

### Sound (not implemented)

For the record: with After Dark's sound extension present, Flap 1, Flap 2
and Mix 1 play back to back, each next one picked at random but never the
same twice running, starting with Flap 1. It is a soundtrack, not tied to
any toaster.

## How it gets built

### Extraction (build time)

- A uv script, `tools/after_dark_sprites.py`, reads the disk image and writes
  a C header of the ten sprites:
  - strips the 12-byte sector tags when the image is 1600 × 524 bytes; also
    accepts a plain 819,200-byte volume;
  - reads the HFS volume and the module's resource fork;
  - decodes the ten PICTs (PackBitsRect, 1-bit and 4-bit indexed with a
    colour table, drawn through `picFrame`);
  - writes 64×64 RGB888 for the colour frames and 1 bit per pixel for the
    mono ones, plus the image's SHA-256 in a comment.
- A PlatformIO pre-script, `firmware/after_dark_sprites.py`, modelled on
  `pacman_sprites.py`:
  - image absent: prints one line saying the toasters are left out, and
    does nothing else;
  - image present: regenerates the header under `$BUILD_DIR/generated/`
    when it is older than the image or the tool, writes through a
    `.partial` file, then adds the include path and defines
    `HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS`;
  - image present but extraction fails: the build fails loudly. A silently
    missing hack would hide a broken tool.
- It is added to `extra_scripts` in all three envs (`stopwatch`, `native`,
  `dump`).
- The image path is fixed: `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k`.

### The hack

- `firmware/src/hacks/toasters/` holds our own code (MIT), not a copy of an
  xscreensaver hack, so the byte-identical rule does not apply and it needs
  no `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` row: nothing in the repo is copied. Its header
  comment credits the original authors and says the art comes from the
  user's own disk at build time.
- Split the simulation (slots, spawning, motion, collision, flap state,
  doneness maths) from the drawing and from the sprite data. Then host tests
  can drive the simulation with stand-in sprites, whether or not the disk is
  present.
- It is a `HackEntry` like the others (init, draw, free), registered in
  `g_hacks[]` under `#ifdef HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS`, **at the end of the
  list**, so every other hack keeps its index for `dump` and the scorer.
- Registry name `toasters`, display name "Flying Toasters". Not
  `flyingtoasters`: the scorer marks an xscreensaver hack ✅ by matching
  names in `g_hacks[]`, and xscreensaver's own unported `flyingtoasters` would
  wrongly show as done.
- At init: pick 1-bit or colour, pick a doneness, build the five 70×70
  sprites (art plus black strips) in RGB565, scatter the 10 flyers, fill the
  screen black and draw them all once. Log the picks on one line (for
  example `toasters: colour, doneness=dark`) so a serial capture says what
  the screen should show.
- Background resource black.

### Choices left to the builder

- How sprites reach the canvas: `XPutImage` through the shim, or a small
  blit straight into the canvas with `canvas_mark_dirty`. Either is fine if
  it stays opaque and marks only the touched rows dirty. Ten 70×70 blits a
  step is about 49,000 pixels; dirty rows keep the push to roughly the rows
  the flyers cover.
- Pacing: the runner waits the returned delay *after* the push, and step
  time is not counted against it (see `main.cpp`). Aim for 30 steps a
  second, and report what the device actually achieves.
- The HFS reader: the `machfs` package worked in the investigation. Check
  its licence before relying on it (it is a tool dependency fetched by uv,
  not copied into the repo); a small reader of our own is the fallback.
- The layout of the generated header.

## Testing

Tests first, as everywhere in this repo, and none may contain Berkeley
bytes.

- Python (`tools/tests`):
  - the PICT decoder and resource-fork parser, against small PICTs and
    resource forks the test builds itself;
  - sector-tag stripping on a synthetic image;
  - one optional test that runs the tool on the real image when it is
    present and checks five colour and five mono 64×64 sprites come out.
    Skipped, not failed, without it.
- C (native, Unity, with stand-in sprites such as solid colours):
  - flap order 0 1 2 3 2 1 0;
  - per-step motion for speeds 1-3;
  - the collision nudge, both branches, and the keep-base-step fallback;
  - removal once off screen and respawn at the top or right edge;
  - initial placement fully inside the bounds;
  - at most 4 placement tries, with the slot left empty and retried;
  - the doneness subtraction, including clamping at 0;
  - the 1-bit expansion to white on black;
  - **trail wiping**: after several steps, every non-black pixel lies inside
    some flyer's current rect.
- Mutation-check the new tests, as `AGENTS.md` asks.
- When the image is present, the suite's every-hack run (3000 frames under
  ASan, leak check across restarts) covers `toasters` too.
- On the device: flash a build pinned with `START_HACK="toasters"` and
  rotation off (ask Rod first), capture `fps=` and `rows=` over a few
  minutes, and report the mean and the worst window. Restart it several
  times so Rod sees both art sets and all three donenesses. Only Rod can
  confirm the look; tell him what to check: the colour toast's shade in the
  logged doneness, and white line art in 1-bit mode.

## Licensing and housekeeping

- Nothing extracted from the disk is committed. The generated header lives
  in the git-ignored build directory, and `vendor/` is already ignored.
- The README gets a short note: Flying Toasters needs your own copy of the
  After Dark 2.0 disk at `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k`, and is left out
  without it.
- `AGENTS.md` gets the new pre-script, the `HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS` define,
  and the rule that `toasters` sits at the end of `g_hacks[]`.
- Check `tools/score_hacks.py` copes with a registered name that is not an
  xscreensaver hack.

## Open questions

- The count slider's range is assumed to be 0-100 (After Dark's usual).
  It only matters if we ever expose the count; with the default 54 the
  answer is 10 either way.
- How often flyers overlap in practice was not simulated. The host tests
  and the device run will show it; it is faithful either way.

Rod, the design is written and committed: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-flying-toasters-design.md`, commit `ebce999` on `feature/flying-toasters-design`, in the `flying-toasters` worktree. It's lint-clean, and a fresh reviewer read it as the person who'd build it; I've folded in what they found.

**Your decisions, as written into the doc:**

- Original 1× sprite size.
- Each start picks 1-bit or colour, and a doneness, at random.
- The art is read at build time from your git-ignored disk image. Without the image the hack is left out of the build.

**My calls, worth checking as you read:**

- **Name:** the overlay and `START_HACK` use `FlyingToasters`, matching the CamelCase of the other hacks. The code symbol is `toasters_hack`, because the scorer would otherwise mark xscreensaver's own unported `flyingtoasters` as done.
- **Real randomness for the two picks:** the reviewer spotted that nothing seeds `random()` on the board, so a pinned build would make the same picks on every boot. The picks will use the chip's hardware random source instead. I deliberately didn't reseed `random()`, because every other hack draws from it.
- **Force flags:** two build flags will force the art and doneness, so you can look at each combination on purpose.
- **Faithful quirks kept:** there's no transparency mask. Each sprite is an opaque block whose black border wipes its own trail, and overlapping flyers can briefly cover each other with black. Doneness only shows in colour, as in the original.
- **No sound,** in line with the project's non-goals. The doc records how the original's sound worked anyway.
- **Placement in the list:** the hack goes at the end of the hack list, so no other hack's index changes in `dump`.
- **Loud failure:** if the image is present but extraction fails, the build fails rather than quietly dropping the hack.

**No Berkeley bytes in git.** The extracted sprites, the disassembly and the subagent's annotated notes stay in this session's scratch folder. The doc has behaviour descriptions and code offsets only.

If the doc reads right to you, the next step is the implementation plan.

Reviewing now.  As a note, the Internet Archive has a copy of the original disk image for download at https://archive.org/details/after-dark-2.0v-800k so we can link there from our docs.

1. Let's call our hack ad-flyingtoasters to acknowledge its After Dark origin and distinguish it from the `flyingtoasters` hack in xscreensaver.
2. The board *does* have a speaker.  I don't think we should port sound over right now, but it's a possible future enhancement.

Otherwise, I think you're good to go
Grand. I'll make those three changes, then move on to the plan.

1	# Flying Toasters from After Dark 2.0: design
2	
3	## Intent
4	
5	Bring back After Dark's Flying Toasters, the classic 1990 Mac screensaver,
6	on the StopWatch, as faithfully as the hardware allows: the original art,
7	moving to the original rules. Rod owns a copy of After Dark 2.0 on an 800K
8	floppy image. This is a nostalgia piece for his own badge, in the same spirit
9	as Pyro was for the xscreensaver hacks.
10	
11	The art and code are Berkeley Systems' copyright and carry no licence to
12	redistribute. The repo is public and MIT. So the design follows the
13	ScummVM model: **our code reproduces the behaviour; the art is read at build
14	time from the user's own disk image, which is never committed.** Anyone
15	without the image gets a build with no toasters in it.
16	
17	## Goals
18	
19	- A new hack, `FlyingToasters`, that reproduces Flying Toasters' motion, spawning,
20	  wing-flap animation, collision nudging and toast doneness, worked out from
21	  the original 68000 code (see "Behaviour" below).
22	- The original sprites, extracted at build time from
23	  `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k`.
24	- Each time the hack starts it picks, at random:
25	  - the **1-bit** or the **16-colour** art (even odds);
26	  - the toast **doneness**: Light, Medium or Dark (even odds).
27	
28	  This is Rod's request: the original made these user settings.
29	- Sprites at their original size, 64×64 (1×). Rod chose this over 2× from
30	  mockups of the round panel.
31	- Builds without the disk image still succeed, and simply leave the hack out.
32	
33	## Non-goals
34	
35	- Sound. The original plays its flap sounds through After Dark's sound
36	  extension; the board has no speaker, and sound is a non-goal for the whole
37	  project. The rule is recorded below for completeness only.
38	- User settings at run time (count, colour, doneness sliders). Count stays at
39	  the original's default; colour and doneness are random per start.
40	- Other After Dark modules. The disk holds 30-odd; they may follow later, and
41	  the extraction tool should not make that harder, but this design covers
42	  only Flying Toasters.
43	- Porting xscreensaver's `flyingtoasters` (jwz's OpenGL tribute). It is a
44	  different look and an XL GL port; it stays unported.
45

226	- In 1-bit mode doneness has no effect, as in the original. The random pick
227	  is still made, so the log can show it, but the toast looks the same.
228	
229	### Sound (not implemented)
230	
231	For the record: with After Dark's sound extension present, Flap 1, Flap 2
232	and Mix 1 play back to back, each next one picked at random but never the
233	same twice running, starting with Flap 1. It is a soundtrack, not tied to
234	any toaster.
235	
236	## How it gets built
237	
238	### Extraction (build time)
239	
240	- A uv script, `tools/after_dark_sprites.py`, reads the disk image and writes
241	  a C header of the ten sprites:
242	  - strips the 12-byte sector tags when the image is 1600 × 524 bytes; also
243	    accepts a plain 819,200-byte volume;
244	  - reads the HFS volume and the module's resource fork;
245	  - decodes the ten PICTs (PackBitsRect, 1-bit and 4-bit indexed with a
246	    colour table, drawn through `picFrame`);
247	  - writes 64×64 RGB888 for the colour frames and 1 bit per pixel for the
248	    mono ones, plus the image's SHA-256 in a comment.
249	- A PlatformIO pre-script, `firmware/after_dark_sprites.py`, modelled on
250	  `pacman_sprites.py`:
251	  - image absent: prints one line saying the toasters are left out, and
252	    does nothing else;
253	  - image present: regenerates the header under `$BUILD_DIR/generated/`
254	    when it is older than the image or the tool, writes through a
255	    `.partial` file, then adds the include path and defines
256	    `HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS`;
257	  - image present but extraction fails: the build fails loudly. A silently
258	    missing hack would hide a broken tool.
259	- It is added to `extra_scripts` in all three envs (`stopwatch`, `native`,
260	  `dump`).
261	- The image path is fixed: `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k`.
262	
263	### The hack
264	
265	- `firmware/src/hacks/toasters/` holds our own code (MIT), not a copy of an
266	  xscreensaver hack, so the byte-identical rule does not apply and it needs
267	  no `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` row: nothing in the repo is copied. Its header
268	  comment credits the original authors and says the art comes from the
269	  user's own disk at build time.
270	- Split the simulation (slots, spawning, motion, collision, flap state,
271	  doneness maths) from the drawing and from the sprite data. Then host tests
272	  can drive the simulation with stand-in sprites, whether or not the disk is
273	  present.
274	- It is a `HackEntry` like the others (init, draw, free), registered in
275	  `g_hacks[]` under `#ifdef HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS`, **at the end of the
276	  list**, so every other hack keeps its index for `dump` and the scorer.
277	- Naming (decided by Claude): the entry's symbol is `toasters_hack`, its
278	  `name` is `"FlyingToasters"`. The name follows the CamelCase of the
279	  others (`UnknownPleasures`, `HexTrail`); it is what the overlay shows, the
280	  serial lines print and `START_HACK` matches, case-insensitively, so pin it
281	  with `START_HACK="flyingtoasters"`. The symbol is not `flyingtoasters_hack`
282	  because the scorer reads registered hacks from the `&<name>_hack` symbols
283	  in `g_hacks[]` (`score_hacks.py`), and xscreensaver's own unported
284	  `flyingtoasters` would wrongly show as done.
285	- **The two picks need real entropy** (decided by Claude). Nothing seeds
286	  `random()` from entropy on the device, so `random()` replays the same
287	  sequence after every boot, and a pinned build would make the same picks
288	  every time. Take the art and doneness picks from `esp_random()` on the
289	  device, behind a small function the host build replaces with `random()`
290	  (host tests then stay deterministic after `srandom(1)`). Do not reseed
291	  `random()` itself: every other hack draws from it, and changing its
292	  sequence would change what they see. Flyer placement and speeds keep
293	  using `random()`, like the original's `Random()`.
294	- Two build flags force the picks, for looking at each combination on the
295	  device: `-DTOASTERS_ART=mono|colour` and `-DTOASTERS_DONENESS=light|medium|dark`
296	  (exact spelling is the builder's). Without them the picks are random.
297	- At init: pick 1-bit or colour, pick a doneness, build the five 70×70
298	  sprites (art plus black strips) in RGB565, scatter the 10 flyers, fill the
299	  screen black and draw them all once. Log the picks on one line (for
300	  example `toasters: colour, doneness=dark`) so a serial capture says what
301	  the screen should show.
302	- Background resource black.
303	
304	### Choices left to the builder
305	
306	- How sprites reach the canvas: `XPutImage` through the shim, or a small
307	  blit straight into the canvas with `canvas_mark_dirty`. Either is fine if
308	  it stays opaque and marks only the touched rows dirty. Ten 70×70 blits a
309	  step is about 49,000 pixels; dirty rows keep the push to roughly the rows
310	  the flyers cover.
311	- Pacing: the runner waits the returned delay *after* the push, and step
312	  time is not counted against it (see `main.cpp`). Aim for 30 steps a
313	  second, and report what the device actually achieves.
314	- The HFS reader: the `machfs` package worked in the investigation. Check
315	  its licence before relying on it (it is a tool dependency fetched by uv,
316	  not copied into the repo); a small reader of our own is the fallback.
317	- The layout of the generated header.
318	
319	## Testing
320	
321	Tests first, as everywhere in this repo, and none may contain Berkeley
322	bytes.
323	
324	- Python (`tools/tests`):
325	  - the PICT decoder and resource-fork parser, against small PICTs and
326	    resource forks the test builds itself;
327	  - sector-tag stripping on a synthetic image;
328	  - one optional test that runs the tool on the real image when it is
329	    present and checks five colour and five mono 64×64 sprites come out.
330	    Skipped, not failed, without it.
331	- C (native, Unity, with stand-in sprites such as solid colours):
332	  - flap order 0 1 2 3 2 1 0;
333	  - per-step motion for speeds 1-3;
334	  - the collision nudge, both branches, and the keep-base-step fallback;
335	  - removal once off screen and respawn at the top or right edge;
336	  - initial placement fully inside the bounds;
337	  - at most 4 placement tries, with the slot left empty and retried;
338	  - the doneness subtraction, including clamping at 0;
339	  - the 1-bit expansion to white on black;
340	  - **trail wiping**: after several steps, every non-black pixel lies inside
341	    some flyer's current rect.
342	- Mutation-check the new tests, as `AGENTS.md` asks.
343	- When the image is present, the suite's every-hack run (3000 frames under
344	  ASan, leak check across restarts) covers `FlyingToasters` too.
345	- Under `#ifdef HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS`, add the hack to
346	  `test_hacks.c`'s expected names and its baselines.
347	- On the device: flash a build pinned with `START_HACK="flyingtoasters"`
348	  and rotation off (ask Rod first), capture `fps=` and `rows=` over a few
349	  minutes, and report the mean and the worst window. Restarts make random
350	  picks, but to show Rod each combination on purpose, flash with the force

352	  look; tell him what to check: the colour toast's shade in the logged
353	  doneness, and white line art in 1-bit mode.
354	
355	## Licensing and housekeeping
356	
357	- Nothing extracted from the disk is committed. The generated header lives
358	  in the git-ignored build directory, and `vendor/` is already ignored.
359	- The README gets a short note: Flying Toasters needs your own copy of the

238	same twice running, starting with Flap 1. It is a soundtrack, not tied to
239	any toaster.
240	
241	## How it gets built
242	
243	### Extraction (build time)
244	
245	- A uv script, `tools/after_dark_sprites.py`, reads the disk image and writes
246	  a C header of the ten sprites:
247	  - strips the 12-byte sector tags when the image is 1600 × 524 bytes; also
248	    accepts a plain 819,200-byte volume;
249	  - reads the HFS volume and the module's resource fork;
250	  - decodes the ten PICTs (PackBitsRect, 1-bit and 4-bit indexed with a
251	    colour table, drawn through `picFrame`);
252	  - writes 64×64 RGB888 for the colour frames and 1 bit per pixel for the
253	    mono ones, plus the image's SHA-256 in a comment.
254	- A PlatformIO pre-script, `firmware/after_dark_sprites.py`, modelled on
255	  `pacman_sprites.py`:
256	  - image absent: prints one line saying the toasters are left out, and
257	    does nothing else;
258	  - image present: regenerates the header under `$BUILD_DIR/generated/`
259	    when it is older than the image or the tool, writes through a
260	    `.partial` file, then adds the include path and defines
261	    `HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS`;
262	  - image present but extraction fails: the build fails loudly. A silently
263	    missing hack would hide a broken tool.
264	- It is added to `extra_scripts` in all three envs (`stopwatch`, `native`,
265	  `dump`).
266	- The image path is fixed: `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k`.
267	
268	### The hack
269	
270	- `firmware/src/hacks/ad_flyingtoasters/` holds our own code (MIT), not a
271	  copy of an xscreensaver hack, so the byte-identical rule does not apply and it needs
272	  no `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` row: nothing in the repo is copied. Its header
273	  comment credits the original authors and says the art comes from the
274	  user's own disk at build time.
275	- Split the simulation (slots, spawning, motion, collision, flap state,
276	  doneness maths) from the drawing and from the sprite data. Then host tests
277	  can drive the simulation with stand-in sprites, whether or not the disk is
278	  present.
